name: Siege of Baghdad (1258)
info: A Mongol army under Hulegu besieged Baghdad, capital of the Abbasid Caliphate, in early 1258; the city surrendered on 10 February, was sacked and the caliph al-Musta'sim was executed, ending the caliphate there.

facts.date: The assault began on either 29 or 30 January 1258; the caliph surrendered on 10 February, the sack began on 13 February and the caliph was executed on 20 February
facts.place: Baghdad on the Tigris, in Mesopotamia, present-day Iraq
facts.sides: The Mongol Empire under the prince Hulegu, with vassal troops from Armenia, Georgia and the Seljuk lands and a corps of engineers, an army put at 138,000, nearly 200,000 or 300,000 men by modern scholars; the Abbasid Caliphate under the caliph al-Musta'sim, with around 30,000 troops left in the city, a garrison given elsewhere as at most 50,000 before the sortie of January
facts.outcome: Baghdad surrendered, was pillaged and its people killed for about a week, and the caliph was executed. The total of the dead is unknown: later Muslim writers say 800,000 to two million, and Hulegu himself claimed two million.

t: The number of dead is unknown. Later Muslim writers put it between 800,000 and two million, Hulegu claimed two million in a letter to Louis IX, and his count has been called obviously inflated.

The Mongols flooded the Abbasid army's camp, enclosed the city with a palisade and moat, breached the walls with siege engines within a few days and refused all terms short of unconditional surrender.
The fall of Baghdad ended the Abbasid Caliphate there, but modern historians call the claim that it ended the Islamic Golden Age simplistic, and large libraries reopened within two years.
dyk: To avoid spilling royal blood, a great taboo for the Mongols, the caliph al-Musta'sim was wrapped in a rolled-up carpet and trampled to death by horses.
ev: Al-Mansur founds Baghdad as the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate
Hulegu sets out from Karakorum with the army assigned to him by his brother Möngke Khan
The Assassins' Grand Master surrenders and Alamut follows, while al-Musta'sim refuses to send troops
Hulegu begins a correspondence with the caliph, who replies defiantly
Baiju's forces flood the Abbasid camp and rout the caliph's army, and Hulegu reaches the city and invests it
The Mongols breach the walls, and the caliph surrenders after unarmed men who came out are executed
The sack lasts about a week, and the caliph is executed on 20 February
Timur's siege is one of those that led to the city's long-term marginalization, with a second in 1401

sections.background:
Baghdad was founded in 762 by al-Mansur, the second Abbasid caliph, who wanted a capital away from threats and near the dynasty's power base in Persia. Wealthy from the trade routes and taxes it controlled, it became a world city and the centre of the Islamic Golden Age, with centres of learning such as the House of Wisdom. In the tenth century the Abbasids lost power; the Buyids occupied Baghdad in 945 and the Seljuks in 1055, when the caliphs held only local authority. The caliphate recovered under al-Nasir (r. 1180–1225).

The Mongols reached the region after the conquest of Khwarazm. From 1230 the general Chormaqan established Mongol hegemony in north-western Iran and the Transcaucasus. They besieged Irbil in 1237 and raided up to Baghdad's walls the next year, but Baghdad remained unconquered and even defeated a Mongol force in 1245.

After Möngke Khan became khan in 1251, he sent his brother Hulegu westwards to destroy the Nizari Ismaili Assassins and secure the submission of the Abbasid caliphs. Hulegu had expected al-Musta'sim to supply troops against the Assassins. The caliph first agreed, but his ministers argued that the request was meant to empty Baghdad of defenders, and he refused. The Assassins' strongholds fell in late 1256.
sections.forces:
Möngke assigned Hulegu one fifth of the empire's manpower, a figure modern scholars have calculated as 138,000, nearly 200,000 or 300,000 men. The army included troops from Armenia under King Hetoum I, a thousand-strong corps of military engineers led by Guo Kan, auxiliaries from across the empire and generals from all branches of the Mongol imperial family, among them three Golden Horde princes. Baiju brought Seljuk, Georgian and Armenian vassals to join it in the summer of 1257.

Baghdad was left with around 30,000 troops. Another figure puts the garrison at no more than 50,000 before the sortie of January, untrained and largely incapable. The walls, weakened by a flood and in disrepair, were in poor shape, and in 1256 sectarian violence between Sunnis and Shi'a had broken out after the flood. Later Sunni writers accused the Shi'ite vizier Muhammad ibn al-Alqami of betraying the caliph through secret talks with Hulegu.

In their exchange of letters, Hulegu demanded that the caliph submit and send his vizier, commander of the soldiers and dawatdar. Al-Musta'sim called Hulegu young and ignorant and said he could summon armies from all of Islam, although the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt was hostile to him and the Ayyubid rulers in Syria were concerned with their own survival. Envoys of Hulegu were mocked by mobs in Baghdad's streets.
sections.course:
Hulegu sacked Kermanshah on 6 December 1257, with Golden Horde princes on his right wing and Kitbuqa on the left in Khuzistan. Baiju crossed the Tigris at Mosul with help from its emir and reached the Nahr Isa canal in mid-January 1258. On 16 January the dawatdar with 20,000 infantry forced his deputy Sughunchaq to retreat. That night Baiju's forces broke the dykes of the Dujayl Canal and flooded the camp of the celebrating Abbasid army. Many drowned, and the rest were routed the next morning.

Hulegu reached the eastern suburbs on 22 January, where he was welcomed by local Shi'ites. The Mongols erected a palisade around the city and dug a moat inside it, finishing both within a day, built mounds for mangonels and ballistae, and used burning naphtha. Pontoon bridges across the Tigris stopped any escape by river. The assault began on 29 or 30 January. Messages guaranteeing safety, including to Christians, were shot into the city by arrow. The first breach, in the Ajami tower on 1 February, was driven back, but further breaches let the Mongols take the east battlements by 4 February. The dawatdar tried to flee by river and was forced back with the loss of three ships.

Envoys, among them al-Alqami and the Patriarch Makkikha II, were sent during the next week. Hulegu insisted on unconditional surrender, especially after one of his commanders was wounded by an arrow during a parley. On 7 February a large number of unarmed soldiers and inhabitants came out, apparently hoping to be spared, and were divided into groups and executed. The caliph surrendered on 10 February with his family and 3,000 dignitaries.
sections.aftermath:
Hulegu asked the caliph to order the population to leave the city after laying down their weapons, and those who obeyed were slaughtered. The sack began on 13 February. Sayyids, scholars, merchants who traded with the Mongols, and Christians, for whom Hulegu's Christian wife Doquz Khatun had interceded, were told to mark their doors so their houses would be spared. The rest of the city was pillaged and its people killed for a full week. Kirakos Gandzaketsi, a 13th-century Armenian historian, says the Christians in Hulegu's army took special pleasure in it.

How many inhabitants were killed is unknown. Later Muslim writers estimated between 800,000 and two million, and Hulegu told Louis IX of France that his army had killed two million, a count described as obviously inflated. An epidemic among the survivors, which scholars have debated as possibly plague, may have raised the figures. A physician who was present recorded that a pestilence killed so many refugees that their bodies could not be buried and were thrown into the Tigris.

On 15 February Hulegu made the caliph reveal his treasures, most of which were sent to Karakorum or to Shahi Island, and gave the palace to Makkikha as a church. On 20 February, after the killing and plundering had stopped, al-Musta'sim was executed with his family and court. Al-Alqami was kept as vizier and died less than three months later. Hulegu stationed 3,000 soldiers in the city, ordered it rebuilt and its bazaars reopened, and left on 8 March.
sections.sources:
Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, who was likely present, recorded the exchange at Hulegu's banquet, in which the caliph, offered a golden tray and told to eat, said it was not edible and that his fate was God's will. A physician who was present recorded the pestilence among the refugees. Kirakos Gandzaketsi, an Armenian historian of the 13th century, wrote that the Christians in Hulegu's army took special pleasure in the sack, and Hulegu's own letter to Louis IX gives his claim of two million dead. The historian René Grousset called the exchange of letters with the caliph one of the most magnificent dialogues in history.

Later Sunni writers accused al-Alqami of treachery, but Mongol policy was to execute traitors, and Hulegu instead reappointed him as vizier. Marco Polo and other Christian writers tell that the caliph was starved to death among his treasures, a folktale likely drawn from the banquet. A 16th-century historian wrote that so many books were thrown into the Tigris that its colour turned black. The start of the assault, 29 or 30 January, is uncertain, and so are the size of the army, the garrison, the deaths and whether plague was the epidemic.
sections.legacy:
The fall of Baghdad ended the 500-year-old Abbasid Caliphate there. A member of the dynasty reached Cairo, where the Mamluks installed him as al-Mustansir II, but he and his descendants were puppets of the Mamluk state and gained little recognition in the wider Muslim world; the Ottomans later usurped them and kept the title of caliph into the 20th century. Power shifted from Baghdad to cities such as Tabriz, capital of the Ilkhanate that Hulegu founded after the siege.

Muslim writers have traditionally blamed this one event for the decline of the Islamic Golden Age and, consequently, the later rise of the West, an argument modern historians have criticised as simplistic and lazy. The historian Michal Biran has shown that large libraries reopened for learning and teaching within two years of the siege. Baghdad prospered under Hulegu's Ilkhanate, though it declined compared with Tabriz, and Hulegu and his successors patronized musical and literary traditions.

According to Biran, it was later sieges, those of Timur in 1393 and 1401 and of the Ottomans in 1534, that ensured the city's long-term marginalization. The sack has been described as a calculated decision to show the consequences of defying the Mongol Empire rather than wanton destruction, and Hulegu is said to have executed the caliph to break the myth of the caliphate as an all-powerful, invulnerable and inviolate entity.

summary: In early 1258 a Mongol army under Hulegu invested Baghdad, breached its walls within days and took the city on 10 February. A week of pillaging and killing followed, with the dead put at 800,000 to two million by later writers, and the caliph al-Musta'sim was executed.
references: Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World: From Conquest to Conversion (Yale University Press, 2017)
Justin Marozzi, Baghdad: City of Peace, City of Blood (Penguin UK, 2014)
Timothy May, The Mongol Empire (Edinburgh University Press, 2018)
George Lane, Early Mongol Rule in Thirteenth-Century Iran: A Persian Renaissance (Routledge, 2003)
notes: Garrison: the lead gives around 30,000 troops, the body says at most 50,000 before the dawatdar's sortie; both are given.
Sortie date: the lead says 17 January, the body has the confrontation on 16 January and the rout the next morning; I used the body.
The article's text 'Christians in Hulegu's army took special pleasure' is Kirakos's claim and attributed.
Left out: the two letters' poetic quotation, the astronomers' prophecy, Monica Green's plague suggestion, the Mongol camp moves, Guo Kan's share of treasure.
The Ev entry for 1393 mentions Timur's siege; the article says 'subsequent sieges like those by Timur in 1393 and 1401'.
